extracted.intended_audience: interested parties, stakeholders, attorneys, advocates, and members of the public who want to participate in California state agency rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and practical guidance for participating in and complying with California state administrative rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), including required documents, notice-and-comment procedures, hearings, and OAL review standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency rulemaking calendar
rubrics_metrics.description: Every state agency is required to annually adopt a 'rulemaking calendar' that is published on their website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must publish a calendar so interested parties can track upcoming regulatory activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interested parties mailing lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies establish interested parties mailing lists for notices of rulemaking activities by that agency or department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders should sign up for agency mailing lists to receive direct notifications of proposed rulemaking and notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with APA procedural requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: California law requires every State agency to satisfy the basic minimum procedural requirements established by the APA for the adoption, amendment or repeal of a regulation, unless the agency is expressly exempted by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must follow prescribed procedures set out in the APA and CCR Title 1; failure to follow procedures can be grounds for challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency cannot exceed its legally-prescribed authority to regulate; the authority to adopt policy is defined and restricted by the authorizing statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations must stay within the scope delegated by the Legislature; courts recognize delegation only where adequate standards are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required preliminary rulemaking documents
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency develops four required documents during the preliminary activity stage: the express terms of the proposed regulation (i.e., the proposed text), the initial statement of reasons, the fiscal impact statement, and the notice of proposed rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These documents are initially filed with OAL and then published by the agency; preparing these correctly is essential to initiating the formal rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and distribution of notice of proposed rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The notice of proposed rulemaking must be published in the California Regulatory Notice Register (CRNR), mailed to interested parties, and posted on the rulemaking agency’s website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication in the CRNR plus direct mailing/website posting triggers the formal comment period and public awareness obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: 45-day written comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 45-day opportunity to submit written, faxed or e-mail comments on all or any part of a proposed rulemaking when the notice of proposed rulemaking is published in the CRNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments can address any aspect of the proposal; timely submission during the 45-day window is required to be considered timely-filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public hearing requirement and request window
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency may choose whether to hold a public hearing, but if it does not schedule one and any interested person submits a written request for one within 15 days prior to the close of the written comment period, the agency must hold a public hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of this automatic-trigger requirement, agencies typically schedule a hearing at the outset. Interested persons should monitor timing and submit hearing requests within the 15-day pre-closure window to compel a hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of all relevant information
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA requires a rulemaking agency to consider all relevant information presented to it during the comment period before adopting, amending or repealing the regulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies must review and weigh timely-filed comments and other materials; failure to consider relevant material can be challenged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notice of opportunity to comment on proposed modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Before adopting regulatory changes, the agency must mail a notice of opportunity to comment on those proposed changes along with a copy of the text of the proposed changes to each person who has submitted written comments on the proposal, testified at the public hearing, or asked to receive a notice of proposed modification; the agency must also post the notice on its website.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When agencies change their proposals after the initial comment period, they must give prior commenters and participants another chance to comment on the modifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary and response to comments on the record
rubrics_metrics.description: A rulemaking agency must summarize and respond on the record to timely filed comments; the summary and response are included as part of the final statement of reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL states the agency must either (1) explain how it has amended the proposal to accommodate the comment or (2) explain the reasons for making no change to the proposal. This demonstrates the agency considered the comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transmission of rulemaking file to OAL and review timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency must transmit its rulemaking file to OAL for review within a year from the date that the notice of proposed rulemaking action was published in the CRNR. OAL then has 30 working days in which to review the rulemaking record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely transmission starts the OAL review clock; parties should be aware of these deadlines for post-adoption oversight and potential challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: OAL's six standards of review
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL reviews the rulemaking file for compliance with the six standards of review: Authority, Reference, Consistency, Clarity, Nonduplication, and Necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OAL's review is procedural—OAL may not substitute its judgment for the rulemaking agency regarding substantive regulatory policy, but will check for these specific legal standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity, rationale, and least burdensome effective alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: According to OAL, 'a regulation must be easily understandable, have a rationale, and be the least burdensome, effective alternative.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations should clearly state requirements, explain the rationale, and select alternatives that achieve the objective while imposing the least burden necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on conflicting or superseding statutes
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation cannot alter, amend, enlarge, or restrict a statute, or be inconsistent or in conflict with a statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulatory language must conform to statutory authority and cannot change the statute's meaning or scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-formal participation opportunities (interested parties process)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties can meet with state agency staff prior to a regulatory project commencing to provide input, and many agencies utilize an 'interested parties process' to review draft rulemaking projects prior to commencement of the formal OAL process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engaging early via meetings or interested parties drafts can influence rule development before formal notices are issued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-formal avenues for challenge and involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Even after the agency or department has completed the rulemaking process, there are opportunities to be involved such as with OAL review, appeal to the Governor’s Office, or challenging the rulemaking in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders can use OAL review determinations, executive appeal, or judicial review to contest regulations that fail to meet legal or procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use OAL resources and checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: OAL’s website includes checklists used by OAL to review regulations, as well as publications such as California Rulemaking Law under the Administrative Procedure Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult OAL checklists and publications to prepare compliant rulemaking documents and anticipate review issues.
